summary: Describes how Provider Backbone Bridging can be combined with Ethernet VPN. Customer MAC addresses are aggregated behind provider backbone MAC addresses, which cuts down the number of BGP MAC advertisement routes, helps with MAC mobility, and avoids flushing customer MAC addresses when the topology changes.

eli5.summary: A big school does not list every student at the front gate. It lists classrooms instead. This does the same for network devices, so the lists stay short.

questions: how does pbb reduce bgp mac advertisements in evpn
how does pbb-evpn reduce bgp routes
how does pbb-evpn handle mac mobility
subtitle: How to give EVPN the MAC-address aggregation of Provider Backbone Bridging, so BGP carries one route per site instead of one per host.

tldr.problem: In plain EVPN, a provider edge router sends a BGP route for every customer MAC address. With millions of virtual machines that is a lot of routes, and every move of a machine causes more routes to be sent.
tldr.mechanism: PBB-EVPN puts Backbone Edge Bridge behavior on the provider edge routers. Customer MAC addresses are learned in the data plane and hidden behind a small number of backbone MAC addresses, and only the backbone MAC addresses are advertised in BGP.
tldr.outcome: The number of MAC Advertisement routes depends on the number of Ethernet segments rather than the number of hosts, customer MAC mobility does not cause new BGP routes, and customer MAC addresses need not be flushed when an all-active multihomed link fails.

today: RFC 7623 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on RFC 7432, and it is still the document that defines PBB-EVPN.

sections.title: Why Combine PBB and EVPN
sections.content:
RFC 7432 defines EVPN, a way to build multipoint Layer 2 VPN services over an MPLS/IP core. It uses BGP to distribute customer MAC address reachability. Provider Backbone Bridging (PBB) is an IEEE architecture where MAC tunneling is used to improve service instance and MAC address scalability.

This document, PBB-EVPN, combines the two. The stated goals are to reduce the number of BGP MAC Advertisement routes by aggregating Customer/Client MAC (C-MAC) addresses behind a Provider Backbone MAC (B-MAC) address, to support C-MAC mobility through that aggregation, to confine C-MAC learning to active flows, to offer per-site policies, and to avoid C-MAC flushing on topology changes.
sections.eli5: Normally every device's name goes on a giant public list. This RFC says: put devices behind a few shared group names instead, and only publish the group names.

sections.title: Requirements Beyond Plain EVPN
sections.content:
PBB-EVPN must meet all the EVPN requirements from RFC 7209, plus five more.

  • Route scalability: an EVPN PE normally sends one BGP MAC Advertisement route per C-MAC. In data center interconnect, the number of virtual machines can be in the millions, so a 'MAC summarization' scheme is required.
  • Mobility: with EVPN, a moving virtual machine's MAC must be sent in a BGP route, or traffic goes to the wrong segment. So MAC prefixes cannot be used. PBB defines a B-MAC address space independent of the C-MAC space.
  • Learning and confinement: in EVPN every PE in an instance learns every C-MAC, even PEs not forwarding to it. These addresses still use memory in the routing information base, so visibility should be limited to PEs actively involved.
  • Per-site policy: control which PEs may forward to or from a site. If policy is needed per C-MAC, the C-MAC should be learned in BGP as in RFC 7432.
  • No C-MAC flushing on link, port or node failure for All-Active multihomed segments.
sections.eli5: The list of device names gets too long, changes too often, and gets shown to people who do not need it. The new design fixes all three.

sections.title: Solution Overview
sections.content:
The solution puts IEEE Backbone Edge Bridge (BEB) functionality on the EVPN PE nodes, like PBB-VPLS does for VPLS PEs. A PE receives 802.1Q Ethernet frames from its attachment circuits, wraps them in a PBB header and forwards them across the IP/MPLS core. The egress PE removes the PBB header after MPLS disposition and delivers the original 802.1Q frame to the customer.

Each PE does four things:

  • Learns C-MAC addresses on attachment circuits in the data plane, as a normal bridge does.
  • Learns remote C-MAC to B-MAC bindings in the data plane from traffic arriving from the core.
  • Advertises its local B-MAC reachability in BGP to all other PEs in the same set of service instances.
  • Builds a forwarding table from remote BGP advertisements that ties remote B-MAC addresses to remote PE IP addresses and MPLS labels.
sections.eli5: Each edge router learns which devices sit behind each group name just by watching traffic. Only the group names are announced to everyone.

sections.title: BGP Route Encoding
sections.content:
PBB-EVPN reuses the BGP routes and attributes of RFC 7432, adapted as follows.

  • Ethernet Auto-Discovery route: not needed, because PBB encapsulation gives the needed indirection and an Ethernet Segment can be represented by a B-MAC. The reserved ESI values 0 and MAX-ESI tell the receiving PE it can resolve the path without waiting for this route.
  • MAC/IP Advertisement route: carries B-MAC addresses, not C-MAC addresses. The MAC address field holds the B-MAC, the Ethernet Tag is 0, and the ESI must be 0 (single-homed segments, or multihomed segments with per-I-SID load-balancing) or MAX-ESI (multihomed segments with per-flow load-balancing). It is tagged with the Route Target of its EVI, which is analogous to a B-VID.
  • Inclusive Multicast Ethernet Tag route: used for multicast pruning per I-SID. The Ethernet Tag field holds the I-SID. It has advantages over MMRP: it scales to many PEs and works with any LSP type, while MMRP only works over P2P pseudowires.
  • Ethernet Segment route and ES-Import Route Target: used as in RFC 7432.
  • MAC Mobility extended community: on a B-MAC route it means all C-MAC addresses tied to that B-MAC, across all I-SIDs, must be flushed.
  • ESI Label and Default Gateway extended communities: not used. Split-horizon filtering is done with the B-MAC source address instead.
sections.eli5: The announcements still use the old message types. Only the contents change: they name the groups, not the individual devices.

sections.title: Multihoming and B-MAC Assignment
sections.content:
Because C-MACs are learned in the data plane, every PE has one or more unicast B-MAC addresses and those are what BGP carries. How B-MACs are assigned matters for multihoming.

All-Active (flow-based load-balancing). All PEs attached to the same CE must share one B-MAC for that site. If they used different ones, a remote PE's table would keep oscillating between them as the CE load-balances. Each site needs its own B-MAC, so PE2 serving two sites in the RFC's example uses two. A remote PE can then load-balance toward a B-MAC across the PEs that advertise it, and if a PE loses its link to the site it just withdraws that B-MAC route. The shared B-MAC can be derived from the CE's LACP System Identifier by flipping the 'Locally Administered' bit. A PE MUST advertise the B-MAC with a downstream-assigned MPLS label.

Single-Active (per-I-SID load-balancing). Each PE in the redundancy group gets its own B-MAC. A PE MAY use a shared B-MAC for all its single-homed and Single-Active segments, or a dedicated one per segment. Dedicated B-MACs mean fewer C-MACs are affected by a flush, at the cost of more BGP advertisements. Designated Forwarder filtering applies to unicast and multicast, in both directions.

Failures. With a shared B-MAC, the failed PE re-advertises the B-MAC route with the MAC Mobility extended community and an incremented counter, which makes remote PEs flush the C-MACs. With a dedicated B-MAC, it just withdraws the route. On node failure, remote PEs purge the routes when the BGP session drops or a route reflector withdraws them. A multihomed Ethernet network is handled the same way as a Single-Active device, with I-SID load-balancing.
sections.eli5: If two doors lead to the same room, both must use the same room name, or visitors get confused about which door to use. If a door breaks, that door just stops announcing the name.

sections.title: Frame Forwarding and Encapsulation
sections.content:
Forwarding is split between a Bridge Module, which hosts the PBB BEB function, and an MPLS Forwarder, which imposes and removes MPLS labels.

For known unicast, the PE PBB-encapsulates the frame using the B-MAC source address of the originating site. The B-MAC destination comes from a lookup of the C-MAC destination, learned from reverse traffic. The frame then gets an LSP tunnel label and an EVPN label for the destination B-MAC. If per-flow load-balancing over ECMP is needed, a flow label goes below the B-MAC label. Unknown unicast uses the same options as multicast.

For multicast and broadcast, the B-MAC destination is chosen from the I-SID. The MPLS Forwarder then either does ingress replication over MP2P or P2P tunnel LSPs, using the label from the Inclusive Multicast Ethernet Tag route, or uses a P2MP tunnel LSP (Inclusive or Aggregate Inclusive trees, or MP2MP with Inclusive trees).

PE nodes MAY also run an ARP/ND proxy that snoops ARP and ND messages, keeps an IP/MAC cache and answers requests locally, flooding only on a miss.
sections.eli5: The edge router puts the message in a bigger envelope addressed to the group name, then sends it over the long-distance road. At the far end the outer envelope is removed.

sections.title: Advantages and Interworking
sections.content:
The number of MAC Advertisement routes now depends on the number of Ethernet segments, not hosts. The RFC says the volume may be multiple orders of magnitude lower than with EVPN.

B-MAC locations are fixed, so C-MAC mobility does not cause new BGP routes. The RFC's example: if an EVPN PE advertises N MAC addresses and 50% move, N/2 more routes are sent. In PBB-EVPN the C-MAC to B-MAC bindings simply update through data-plane learning. PEs not in active conversations purge unused C-MACs and keep no control-plane record of them.

For interworking, B-MAC addresses must be globally unique across PBB-EVPN and IEEE 802.1aq / 802.1Qbp networks, and B-MACs of 802.1aq switches are advertised with the EVPN MAC/IP route. With PBB-EVPN the 802.1aq encapsulation can be carried across the MPLS backbone, keeping C-MACs hidden from the PEs. Per-site policy works by giving each site its own B-MAC. For an All-Active segment, if a link fails, the PE withdraws its B-MAC routes and the remote PE keeps one adjacency, with no C-MAC flush.
sections.eli5: Short lists, fewer updates when things move, and no need to forget everything when one road closes.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content:
All security considerations in RFC 7432 apply, since this document uses a subset of its control plane. The RFC says it adds no new security considerations beyond those of RFC 7432 and RFC 4761: B-MAC addresses are handled as in RFC 7432, and C-MAC addresses as in RFC 4761, with B-MACs learned in the control plane and C-MACs learned in the data plane.

There are no IANA considerations beyond what RFC 7432 already describes.
sections.eli5: It uses the same locks as the system it builds on, and adds no new doors.
